title: Honor your parents (Exodus 20:12)
tomorrow: and when honoring a parent would hurt you?

cards: Every family group chat has an order: who hears the news first, whose name comes first on the card. The Torah has an odd one. In the Ten Commandments, the JPS translation reads: "Honour thy father and thy mother."
Father first. A few books later, Leviticus says: "Ye shall fear every man his mother, and his father." Mother first.
Same two parents, flipped. A slip of the pen? The rabbis didn't believe the Torah slips.

teach.h: EACH VERSE LEANS THE OTHER WAY.
teach.b: The Talmud, in tractate Kiddushin, solves it. A child tends to honor the mother more, it says, because she wins him over with words, so in the verse about honor the father comes first.

A child tends to fear the father more, because he teaches him Torah, so in the verse about fear the mother comes first. Each verse leans where the child leans least. The flip is the point: both parents get both.
Then the Talmud gets concrete about the two words.

teach.h: MORA: REVERENCE IN WORD AND PLACE.
teach.b: Fear, mora, is reverence: don't stand in your parent's place or sit in their seat, don't contradict their words, don't settle their arguments as if you were the judge.
Honor, kibbud, is care: food and drink, clothes, a hand coming in and going out. One is how you speak. The other is what your hands do.
Notice what the commandment doesn't ask. It doesn't ask you to agree with them about everything, or to feel a certain way.
It asks for deeds and respect.

And it comes with a promise attached: "that thy days may be long." Something to tell a friend tonight: the Torah names the parents in opposite order in two places, and the rabbis read it as a lesson in balance.

how: Jewish law treats honoring parents as practical care (helping with food, clothing and getting around) and reverence (not sitting in a parent's seat or contradicting them in public); it applies to adult children too, and continues after death, when children mark a parent's yahrzeit.

o: obeying every rule a parent sets, at any age
a blessing children say over their parents
caring for your parents in deed and respect

games.q: two verses, two words — tap the pairs.
p: care: food, clothes, a helping hand

s: the Torah always names the father before the mother
Leviticus 19:3 puts the mother first; Exodus 20:12 puts the father first.
honoring a parent means agreeing with everything they say
the Talmud asks for deeds and reverence, not agreement.
in Kiddushin, honor includes food, clothes and help coming and going
kibbud is care; mora is reverence.

games.q: your dad insists on driving at night even though his eyes have gotten worse. with honor and reverence both in mind, what fits?
o: offer to drive, and raise it with him privately.
take his keys in front of the whole family.
say nothing; any disagreement breaks reverence.
games.why: care is kibbud: you can drive. reverence is mora: don't contradict him in front of others. a private, gentle word keeps both.

practice: Open a message to a parent, or to someone who raised you, and write one line of kibbud: an offer to bring something, fix something, carry something. Read it back once, slowly.
If your parents have died, write it to an elder who's still here, or simply hold their memory while you write.

wordCard.voice: Kibbud av va'em: honoring father and mother. In the Talmud, it's what your hands do, with reverence in what you say.

carryVoice: For the road: honor them, with your hands and with your words. Day three of home and family, honored.

sources.q: Honour thy father and thy mother
Ye shall fear every man his mother, and his father
that thy days may be long

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 30b–31a (why the order flips) and 31b (what fear and honor are)
